# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning}
**THIS BOOK IS A WORK IN PROGRESS. IT IS INCOMPLETE AND MAY HAVE TYPOGRAPHICAL AND OTHER ERRORS. IT IS NOT YET READY TO BE STUDIED FROM.**
:::

[بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم]{.aralt}

The primary texts of [#islAm]{.trn2} (the [#qurEAn]{.trn2} and the [#HadIv]{.trn2}) are in Arabic.
So too is much of its scholarly literature.
However, there are many Muslims for whom Arabic is not a native language, yet who are familiar enough with English to study textbooks written in this language.
The goal of this book is to help them learn Arabic so that,
together with a study of the appropriate expositional texts,
they can start to understand the primary texts in their original language.
We hope that this will, if [#allAh]{.trn2} wills, make them more connected to the primary texts and their teachings.
Furthermore, they can be empowered to study the vast body of Arabic [#islAm]{.trn2}ic literature.

Regarding the title of this book: 
the Arabic grammarians were describing the Arabic language of the time of the Prophet [ﷺ ]{.areng} and his companions.
They were doing this by
drawing upon a corpus that included transmitted texts and the dialectal speech of informants.
The grammarians called this language [العَرَبِيَّة]{.ar} (_[al-#earabiyyah]{.trn2}_).
We term this language _Classical Arabic_,
because of its considerable volume and its agreed upon significance and eloquence.
In the process of the grammarians' sifting through and describing the dialectal variation of Classical Arabic,
a standard variety slowly emerged and gained prevalence. 
Thereafter, texts tended to be composed in an attempt to conform to the grammar of this converging standard.
And it is the grammar of this _Standard Classical Arabic_ ([sca]{.smallcaps}) that is the subject of this work.

The term _Classical Arabic_ has been used by others to refer to the later (non-native) use of what we call [sca]{.smallcaps}.
They may then refer to the language of the grammarians' corpus as pre-Classical Arabic or Old Arabic.
Our choice of terminology is based on the contention that what we call
[sca]{.smallcaps} is but a variety of the native Classical Arabic of the pre-[#islAm]{.trn2}ic and early [#islAm]{.trn2}ic era,
even,
if it was standardized after the native era of Classical Arabic.

[sca]{.smallcaps},
as a standard,
is not precisely defined in its entirety.
There is a core, which is more or less converged upon,
but
there are also dialectal and rare usages
that are occasionally found in some texts.
We cover some of these variations in this book,
depending on how likely we deem the learner to come across them.

We also include in this book post-classical vocabulary, even though it is not, strictly speaking, [sca]{.smallcaps}.
This is because one of our goals is to enable the reader to engage with [#islAm]{.trn2}ic texts.
However, we stop short of dealing with Modern Standard Arabic ([msa]{.smallcaps}).
This is
because the preponderance of its modern vocabulary would detract from the main focus of this book.
And also because Western grammar works which focus on
[msa]{.smallcaps}
tend to use modern texts as a corpus to re-describe and re-codify its grammar.
Which is fine, as a methodology, because their goal is to understand the meaning of 
[msa]{.smallcaps}
texts.
But if we were to include
[msa]{.smallcaps},
as thus defined,
in this book,
then we would have to explain the conflicts between it and
[sca]{.smallcaps}.
Which is something we are not ready,
or equipped,
to deal with.

Part\ I of
this book is a learning or teaching grammar, as opposed to being strictly a reference grammar.
Therefore, whenever we were able to, we have tried to explain topics, and give examples,
in a manner that assumes an understanding of only preceding content.
Part\ II delves into more detail on topics covered only introductorily in part\ I,
and also treats other, more theoretical topics.

We have also aimed to make this a self-instruction textbook so that a diligent student should, if [#allAh]{.trn2} wills, be able to study it independently.
The target learner is someone who has not been exposed to grammatical terminology beyond a grade school level.
While terminology is necessary for a rigorous non-immersive learning of language, we have tried to steer away from Latin-based terms like _accusative_, _jussive_, etc.
Such terms, when first encountered by an uninitiated learner, may deter him from proceeding further.
So we have in some places translated the meaning of Arabic grammar terms to English.
In other places, we have used established English grammar terms where the terms are basic enough.
We have even, in places, invented terms where we deemed appropriate.
We have also used some grammatical terminology from Arabic directly,
usually in cases where our target learner may have already been exposed to them from [#qurEAn]{.trn2} recitation rules,
or where the term is complex enough that creating a term specifically in English wouldn't make it any simpler.
The drawback to this non-standard approach,
however,
is that the student may not be able to immediately relate the terminology he has learned in this book to established terminology in other grammar textbooks.
To remedy this to some extent,
we provide a glossary which maps the grammatical terminology used in this book to other,
established, Latin-based and Arabic-based counterparts.

Because this is an instructional textbook, we have generally avoided quoting verbatim
when drawing material from cited sources, 
But we haven't shied away from sticking close to the cited text when we felt we could not better its expression or organization for our purposes.
Citations are absent for basic topics, and also where we were not able to find an exact reference for some point that we are trying to make.
In any event, any errors that remain in this book are our own.

#### Transcription and translation format {.unnumbered}

* Transcription is in _italics_.
  Word-initial [sukUn]{.trn2} and connecting-hamzah are transcripted using a hyphen.
* Translation is enclosed in  guillemets ([]{.trans}).
  Names in the translation are not italicized.
  For Arabic names in translations and within running English text:

  + The definite article always starts with a [a]{.trans},
    is not capitalized,
    is followed by a hyphen,
    and is not assimilated for "sun-letters."
  + Word final [ي]{.ar}-of-affiliation is transliterated with [[I]{.trn2}]{.trans} instead of [[iyy]{.trn2}]{.trans}.
  + Word-initial hamzah is not transliterated.

For example:

(@) [رَضِيُّ الدِّينِ الْأَسْتَرَابَاذِيُّ]{.ar}  
    [raDiyyu -ddIni -lEastarAbApiyyu]{.trn}  
    [[#raDiyy al-#dIn al-#astarAbApI]{.trn2}]{.trans}

#### Miscellaneous {.unnumbered}

* This book is produced using the [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) authoring and publishing framework and set in the Charis, Vazirmatn, Kitab, and Amiri typefaces.
* Unless otherwise indicated, translations from the [#qurEAn]{.trn2} are by [#SaH]{.trn2}ee[H]{.trn2} International™, sourced from [quran.com](https://quran.com/).
* Unless otherwise indicated, the numbering of cited [#HadIv]{.trn2} is that used by [sunnah.com](https://sunnah.com) and [hadithunlocked.com](https://hadithunlocked.com/).
* The page numbers for citations may vary across different editions and publishers. We have attempted to specify the editions that we are using in the [references](#chap-references).
